t: Speaker & Deputy Speaker (Art. 178): Elected by the Assembly from among its members.
Resignation (Art. 179): The Speaker submits resignation to the Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker.

Continuation After Dissolution (Universal Trap): When the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker does NOT vacate office immediately; continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly.
Voting: Speaker cannot vote in the first instance, but exercises a casting vote in case of an equality of votes (tie).

Disqualification Deciding Authority (Art. 192 vs 10th Schedule): Ordinary Disqualifications (Art. 191/192): Decided by the Governor, who must obtain and act according to the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India.
Disqualification Deciding Authority (Art. 192 vs 10th Schedule): Defection Disqualifications (10th Schedule): Decided exclusively by the Speaker (subject to judicial review).
Sessions & Dissolution (Art. 174): The Governor summons, prorogues, and dissolves the Assembly (maximum session gap: 6 months).
Governor's Address (Art. 176): Addressed at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.
Money Bills (Arts. 198 & 199): Introduced only in the Assembly with prior recommendation of the Governor (Art. 207); Speaker's certification is final; Legislative Council has 14 days.
Ordinary Bills (Art. 197): Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for a maximum of 4 months (3 months first time + 1 month second time); Council cannot permanently block legislation.
Assent & Reservation (Arts. 200 & 201): Governor can give assent, withhold assent, return an ordinary Bill (no fixed time limit), or reserve the Bill for Presidential consideration.
Ordinance Power (Art. 213): Promulgated during legislative recess; ceases to operate 6 weeks after the reassembly of the State Legislature unless approved earlier.
Ministry Size & Non-Member Ministers (Art. 164): Council of Ministers capped at max 15% of Assembly strength (91st CAA, 2003); minimum 12 ministers (including CM).
Ministry Size & Non-Member Ministers (Art. 164): A non-member minister can hold office for a maximum of 6 consecutive months without getting elected.

Article 169 (Council Creation/Abolition): Initiated by Assembly passing a resolution by Special Majority (majority of total membership + ≥2/3 present and voting) enacted into law by Parliament by Simple Majority.
6 Bicameral States: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
Term Extension during National Emergency: Parliament can extend the Assembly term for 1 year at a time, up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases.

t: Prohibition vs Certiorari: Prohibition: Issued to PREVENT -- Operates while the judicial/quasi-judicial proceeding is pending to halt excess of jurisdiction.
Prohibition vs Certiorari: Certiorari: Issued to CORRECT/QUASH -- Operates after the order has been passed to remove or quash decisions suffering from jurisdictional error.
Habeas Corpus vs Mandamus: Habeas Corpus targets illegal custody of a Person (remedy for bodily freedom).
Habeas Corpus vs Mandamus: Mandamus targets non-performance of a Legal Duty by a public authority.
Mandamus vs Quo-Warranto: Mandamus commands: "Perform your lawful public duty."
Mandamus vs Quo-Warranto: Quo-Warranto challenges: "Show your legal qualification/title to hold this public office."
Private Individuals: Habeas Corpus is the only writ directly applicable against private individuals in cases of illegal confinement.
Government Companies (IAS Trap): Mandamus can lie against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function.
Locus Standi Exception: In Quo-Warranto, any member of the public can file a petition (traditional locus standi is relaxed; the petitioner does not need to be personally aggrieved).

t: Collective Responsibility Trap: Ministers are collectively responsible ONLY to the Lower House (Art. 75(3) to Lok Sabha; Art. 164(2) to Legislative Assembly)—NOT to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole, or the President/Governor.
Pleasure of Office: Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President / Governor, NOT the pleasure of the Prime Minister / Chief Minister.
Ordinary Bill Delay: Legislative Council cannot veto or permanently block an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly; it can only delay it for a maximum of 4 months (3 + 1 months).
Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part V (Articles 74, 75, 77, 78); the Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head aids and advises the President of India.
Appointment (Art. 75(1)): Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other Union Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
Tenure (Art. 75(2)): Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Trap: Legally holds office during the pleasure of the President, NOT the Prime Minister).
Oath: The President administers both the Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy under the Third Schedule.
Executive Head vs Head of State: Executive power is constitutionally vested in the President (Head of State) under Art. 53; the Prime Minister is the Head of Government.
House Membership: A Union Minister can be a member of either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (No requirement to be a Lok Sabha member).

Non-Member Ministers: A person who is not a member of either House can be appointed as a Minister, but must become a member within 6 consecutive months; otherwise, ceases to be a Minister (Art. 75(5)).
Speaking vs Voting Rights (Art. 88 Trap): Right to speak and participate in proceedings of both Houses & Joint Sittings -- YES
Speaking vs Voting Rights (Art. 88 Trap): Right to vote in the House of which the Minister is NOT a member -- NO (Can vote ONLY in the House where they hold membership).

Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3)): If the government loses a vote of confidence/majority in Lok Sabha, the entire Council must resign ("Sink or swim together").
Individual Responsibility: Ministers are answerable to Parliament for administrative/bureaucratic lapses under their respective portfolios.
15% Ceiling Limit (91st CAA, 2003): Union (Art. 75(1A)): Total number of Union Ministers, including the PM, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

Prime Minister's Duties (Art. 78): PM communicates all decisions and administrative proposals to the President and submits any matter decided by an individual minister for Council consideration if required by the President.
Confidence vs No-Confidence Motion: Confidence Motion: Moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority.
Confidence vs No-Confidence Motion: No-Confidence Motion: Moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (Rule 198).

Deputy Prime Minister Post: An extra-constitutional / non-constitutional post created for political convenience; carries the status of a Cabinet Minister without superior prime-ministerial powers (First Deputy PM: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, 1947–1950).
Core Mandate: The institutional system governing the appointment and transfer of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

Origin & Status: It is NOT a constitutional body (not expressly mentioned in the Constitution) and was NOT created by an Act of Parliament—it is a judicially evolved system developed through Supreme Court rulings.
Appointing Authority (Art. 124(2) & 217(1)): Judges are formally appointed by the President of India based on the binding recommendations of the Collegium.
Functional Scope: Covers both Appointments (Supreme Court & High Courts) and Transfers (High Court Judges).

under: Evolution: The Three Judges Cases Chain
t: First Judges Case (1981 – S.P. Gupta v. Union of India): Held that "consultation" does NOT mean "concurrence"; established Executive primacy in judicial appointments.

under: Evolution: The Three Judges Cases Chain
t: Second Judges Case (1993 – SCAORA v. Union of India): Reversed the 1981 ruling; held that "consultation" means concurrence; established Judicial primacy and formally birthed the Collegium system (1993).

under: Evolution: The Three Judges Cases Chain
t: Third Judges Case (1998 – Presidential Reference): Clarified procedural working; established that the CJI's opinion must reflect a plural consultation with senior colleagues (expanded the SC Collegium).

NJAC Striking Down Grounds: Struck down in 2015 because executive involvement infringed upon the Independence of the Judiciary, which is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
